name: Weight loss for chin definition

lead: Lowering overall body fat reduces fullness under the chin, so the chin and jawline look sharper. It works on the covering fat, not on bone structure.

A double chin can come from subcutaneous fat around the neck creating a fold, or from jaw bones that do not project far enough forward, often in people of normal weight. Where the cause is fat, losing fat shrinks the fat cells under the chin along with the rest of the body. No study has tested weight loss specifically for chin appearance, and the sources reviewed do not address whether fat can be lost from the chin area selectively.

paras: People reduce body fat through diet and training over weeks to months and watch the jawline and under-chin area in side-view photos. Surgical fat removal and jaw or chin surgery are described for those whose double chin is fat or bony.
No risks specific to this approach are described in the sources reviewed. When the cause is bone structure, fat loss does not change the chin's projection.

web.title: Losing weight can make you more attractive, experts say - but there's a catch
Effects of Bariatric Surgery on Facial Features

angle.text: Lowering body fat reduces fullness under the chin, so the chin and jawline show more clearly, mainly where a double chin is soft tissue. It changes the covering fat rather than bone structure. No studies test fat loss specifically for chin definition.

lead: Weight loss for chin definition is the approach of reducing overall body fat so that the area under the chin and along the jaw looks leaner and the chin and jawline stand out more. People use it to reduce a soft, rounded under-chin fold, often called a double chin, and to make the jaw outline sharper in photos and in person.[1]

Wikipedia describes two different causes of a double-chin look: in some overweight people, fat beneath the chin forms a fold, while in others, often of normal weight, the jaw bones do not project far enough forward so that the chin appears to blend into the neck.[1] Weight loss is relevant to the first type, and surgery such as genioplasty or jaw advancement is described for the second.[1][2]

Researchers at the University of Toronto digitally altered face photos and reported that a BMI change of about 1.33 kg/m2 was needed before people noticed a change in facial weight, and roughly twice that before faces looked more attractive.[3] A small study of gastric-bypass patients found modestly higher attractiveness ratings after about 20 percent weight loss.[4]
infobox: Soft-tissue fat versus bony chin deficiency[1]
About 1.33 BMI points in one photo study[3]

paras: According to Wikipedia, the soft-tissue form is attributed to excess subcutaneous fat around the neck, whereas the bone form occurs in people of normal weight when the jaw bones are insufficiently projecting.[1] Subcutaneous fat is distributed unevenly through the body, with the number of fat cells varying by region and their size changing with nutritional state.[5] Because of this, how much leanness shows in the face varies by person.

sections.h: How weight loss affects the face
paras: In the Toronto photo study by Nicholas Rule and Daniel Re, published in Social Psychological and Personality Science, participants compared digitally altered faces; a BMI change of about 1.33 was needed to notice a difference in weight, and a decrease of about 2.38 (women) or 2.59 (men) before faces looked more attractive, equal to roughly 6.3 kg or 8.2 kg for average-height people.[3] Rule said people need to lose about twice as much for others to find them more attractive.[3] Because the faces were digitally altered, the figures come from simulated faces rather than people who lost weight.[3]

Wikipedia lists surgical removal of the fat pad with a hyoid lift for the soft-tissue form and genioplasty or orthognathic surgery for bony deficiency.[1] Chin augmentation can be done by implants, sliding genioplasty or fillers.[2]

A 2015 Archives of Plastic Surgery study of 14 Roux-en-Y gastric bypass patients at Boston Medical Center, with mean weight loss of 20 percent, had online respondents rate before and after photos. Post-operative photos scored on average 0.256 points higher for attractiveness, while perceived age went up for six patients and down for five, and BMI change did not correlate significantly with either measure.[4] No study found tests lifestyle weight loss specifically for chin or jawline definition.
